tier_reason: results/cascadelake/cascadelake-Xeon-Gold-6240-gcc-8.3.0.rst states the CPU (Xeon Gold 6240), compiler (gcc 8.3.0) and instruction set, and its table shows avx512-harley-seal 0.04826 s and avx2-harley-seal 0.09748 s against the scalar POPCNT loop (cpu) 0.17391 s at 4096 B; the harness is the public speed.cpp and the flags come from the public Makefile in force when the file was generated (ba36276, Dec 2019, unchanged until Aug 2023: -std=c++11 -O2 -mpopcnt -fabi-version=6 -mavx512bw).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 6240, gcc 8.3.0, 4096 B: avx512-harley-seal 0.04826 s versus cpu (64-bit POPCNT loop) 0.17391 s and builtin-popcnt 0.25037 s, about 3.6x and 5.2x; avx2-harley-seal 0.09748 s versus cpu 0.17391 s, about 1.8x; against the fastest scalar row (builtin-popcnt-unrolled-errata 0.16751 s) about 3.5x for AVX-512 and 1.7x for AVX2 (all derived from page data). The POPCNT loop wins up to 512 B: avx512-harley-seal 2.99407 s versus cpu 0.30912 s at 32 B and 0.25122 s versus 0.16864 s at 512 B; the AVX-512 version first wins at 1024 B (0.09325 s versus 0.19950 s). Haswell i7-4770, gcc 5.3.0: avx2-harley-seal 0.11145 s versus cpu 0.19857 s at 4096 B, about 1.8x (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.0 (crosstool-NG 1.24.0) for the Cascade Lake run (2021-02-24). Flags are not printed in the result file; the Makefile in force at that date (commit ba36276, 2019-12-08; next Makefile change 2023-08-20) sets -std=c++11 -O2 -Wall -pedantic -Wextra -Wfatal-errors -mpopcnt -fabi-version=6 plus -mavx512bw -DHAVE_AVX512BW_INSTRUCTIONS for the AVX512BW target (the current Makefile uses -std=c++17).
corrections.caveats: Result files are old (Haswell 2016-03-26 with GCC 5.3.0; Cascade Lake 2021-02-24 with GCC 8.3.0) and were run by the authors; flags are inferred from the Makefile of the time, not printed in the result file. The speed.cpp harness re-counts one cache-resident buffer filled with i & 0xFF for a fixed iteration count, so the tables measure L1-hot throughput. Baseline is the scalar POPCNT instruction loop, a strong baseline; SIMD wins only from about 1 KB on Cascade Lake (AVX-512 Harley-Seal is about 10x slower than POPCNT at 32 B and still slower at 512 B). This repo is sample/benchmark code for the Mula, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions' (arXiv 1611.07612, Computer Journal 2018; paper not opened, arXiv blocked); the packaged library form is kimwalisch/libpopcnt (already listed in wave 11).

notes: Numbers verified on the Cascade Lake and Haswell result files; the record's crossover was slightly off (POPCNT wins through 512 B, not only 32-256 B) and is corrected. Not a duplicate of libpopcnt (wave 11): this is the original harness and algorithm source, libpopcnt is the library that adopted the algorithms; the orchestrator may want to cross-link them. Last commit 2024-04-01 (RISC-V Vector implementation), 357 stars, BSD-2-Clause confirmed.

tier_reason: The 4x over GNU std::sort and 1.4x over Intel IPP figures come only from the IJACSA 2017 / arXiv 1704.08579 abstract, seen in search snippets (arXiv, ar5iv, thesai.org and gitlab.inria.fr all fail DNS here); the repo's paper branch carries the full benchmark harness (main.cpp timeAll against std::sort and IPP) and build lines but no results, so tier C until the paper's tables, CPU model and compiler version are read.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper-branch main.cpp header gives the Skylake build line: g++ -DNDEBUG -O3 -funroll-loops -faggressive-loop-optimizations -std=c++11 -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512bw -mavx512dq -fopenmp (an icpc -O3 -xCOMMON-AVX512 -xCORE-AVX512 -qopenmp alternative is also listed; -DUSE_IPP links IPP). Which compiler and version produced the paper's numbers is not confirmed (paper not opened).
corrections.workload: Paper-branch main.cpp timeAll: single-threaded sort (NewQuickSort512 V1-V5 QsSequential) of random int or double arrays (drand48()*size) from 64 to 2^30 elements in x8 steps, 5 runs (min, max and mean recorded), against std::sort with a lambda less-than comparator and Intel IPP ippsSortRadixAscend (radix sort); a timeAll_pair variant covers int key/value pairs.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the IJACSA 2017 paper and arXiv 1704.08579 were unreachable (thesai.org, arxiv.org, ar5iv and gitlab.inria.fr fail DNS here), so the 4x and 1.4x abstract figures, the Skylake CPU model and the compiler version are unchecked. The 'paper' branch (LICENSE and a 1 MB main.cpp) holds the benchmark harness with build lines but no result tables; the measured code is the paper-branch NewQuickSort512 variants, while master ships a cleaned header library (sort512.hpp, sort512kv.hpp) that was not re-benchmarked, and a 2022-06-20 master commit ('Reverse min params to manage -0/+0') changed signed-zero handling after the paper. IJACSA is a low-selectivity open-access venue. Only AVX-512 (Skylake, earlier Knights Landing report) is covered. The algorithm is cited as reference [2] in numpy/x86-simd-sort (src/xss-common-qsort.h), which is already listed in wave 1 and is the maintained successor.

notes: Metadata confirmed (MIT, 29 stars, last commit 2022-06-20, abandoned). The record's statement that the paper branch has no numbers is right, but it does carry the full benchmark harness and build flags, so a B or A retier is possible once the IJACSA paper (CPU model, compiler) can be opened. baseline_in_list set to true because std::sort (libstdc++) is the C++ incumbent and a scalar C++ reference.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the peer-reviewed InPar 2012 paper (Pharr and Mark, copy at ispc.github.com/papers/ispc_inpar_2012.pdf) Table 2 shows single-core ispc speedups of 3.24x-7.43x over serial non-SIMD C++ on the example workloads in the repo's examples/ directory; not A because the CPU is only '4-core 3.4GHz Core-i7' (no model) and no flags are given.

corrections.claimed_speedup: InPar 2012 paper Table 2 (4-core 3.4 GHz Core i7 iMac, 8-wide AVX), versus serial non-SIMD C++: 1 core / 1 thread aobench 5.58x, Binomial Options 4.39x, Black-Scholes 7.43x, Mandelbrot 5.85x, Ray Tracer 6.85x, Stencil 3.37x, Volume Rendering 3.24x (geomean about 5.0x, derived from page data); 4 cores / 8 threads 12.03x-34.82x. Table 3 (40-core Xeon E7-8870, SSE4, 80 threads, MSVC 2010 serial baseline): 9.40x-243.18x. SSE to AVX geomean 1.42x. README: 'frequently provides a 3x or more speedup on architectures with 4-wide vector SSE units and 5x-6x on architectures with 8-wide AVX vector units'. ispc.github.io/perf.html (gcc 4.2.1 serial baseline on the same iMac): 1 core 3.60x-8.45x, 4 cores 15.53x-33.43x.
corrections.workload: The example programs in the repo's examples/ directory (aobench, binomial and Black-Scholes options pricing, Mandelbrot, ray tracer, 3D stencil, volume rendering; perf page adds deferred shading and Perlin noise), each timed against its included serial C++ reference (minimum of several runs; the examples print '(N.NNx speedup from ISPC)').
corrections.compiler_and_flags: ispc of 2011-2012 (built on LLVM); serial C++ baseline compiled with clang built from the same LLVM (paper notes gcc gave essentially the same results); 40-core runs used MSVC 2010; perf page used gcc 4.2.1 (OS X 10.7.2). Optimization flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: 4-core 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 Apple iMac with AVX (exact model not stated; first-generation AVX, Sandy Bridge era) for Table 2 and the perf page; 2-way hyper-threaded 40-core Intel Xeon E7-8870 at 2.40 GHz with SSE4 on Windows Server 2008 for Table 3.
corrections.caveats: Evidence is from ISPC's Intel authors: a peer-reviewed paper (InPar 2012) plus Intel's perf page, both measured around 2011-2012 on first-generation AVX and SSE4 hardware with an unnamed Core i7 model, unstated flags and an unstated ispc version; nothing newer is published. The baseline is serial non-SIMD C++ (both versions 'received equivalent amounts of performance tuning'), not hand-written intrinsics or SIMD libraries (Highway, xsimd); the paper gives only user anecdotes for intrinsics parity (0.99x-1.05x). Multi-core figures combine task parallelism and hyper-threading with SIMD. ispc is a compiler for an SPMD C dialect, not an intrinsics library, so the category fit is loose. The ispc.github.io perf page was read from its source in the ispc/ispc.github.com repo (github.io blocked here).

notes: Upgrade to B on the peer-reviewed InPar 2012 paper, reached via raw.githubusercontent.com/ispc/ispc.github.com/main/papers/ispc_inpar_2012.pdf; the README claim is a summary of those numbers (single-core geomean about 5.0x on AVX). Metadata confirmed: BSD-3-Clause, 3.0k stars, last commit 2026-10-10, active, not a fork. Benchmark code is public (examples/cpu/*/ with serial references), so an A retier would need a modern run with CPU model and flags.
